title: I built a macro MCP for trading agents — the hardest part was deciding when it should refuse to answer
author: cocopierlab
selftext:
https://preview.redd.it/ke7yxip8m8uh1.png?width=1200&format=png&auto=webp&s=5d239548ba55d4afe721c5f4fd84d5a326176c2d

The screenshot is a real example.

I asked FX Context to find historical analogs for the latest US PCE release and show how EURUSD reacted after similar events.

It refused.

The reason was explicit:

* only **6 usable PCE calibration events**
* **12 are required**
* each event needs at least **3 comparable metrics**

So instead of fabricating an analog, it returned what it could verify: the latest PCE release, the absence of a valid pre-release consensus, and the actual EURUSD reaction after the release.

That’s the design philosophy behind **FX Context**.

It’s an MCP server for FX macro context covering:

* US CPI, NFP and PCE
* Fed, ECB, BOE and BOJ statements
* actual vs. consensus and surprise where provenance is valid
* historical EURUSD / GBPUSD / USDJPY reaction windows
* upcoming macro risks
* historical analogs when there is enough calibration data

A lot of the work has gone into making failure states explicit:

* not enough historical samples → return the actual sample count and threshold
* market closed during a reaction window → return `MARKET_CLOSED`
* no verified pre-release consensus → say so instead of calculating a fake surprise
* incomplete data → preserve provenance and timestamps rather than silently filling gaps

No predictions and no trade signals.

The goal is to keep the deterministic parts inside the data layer:

`event → actual → consensus → surprise → market reaction → agent reasoning`

and let the model focus on interpretation.

Known gaps: PCE consensus coverage is still incomplete, PCE historical analogs are calibration-gated, and NFP consensus coverage is patchy.

I’m the author. It’s closed source, free to use, and there’s no signup:

[`https://fx.coco-pier.com/mcp`](https://fx.coco-pier.com/mcp)

I’m especially interested in feedback on the tool descriptions, response contract, and failure modes — particularly where an agent should refuse to answer instead of trying to infer around missing data.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: refusing when the analog set is thin beats answering, an agent will happily size a trade off three samples. same idea in something I built, Quantradin: trading agents read everything there, and the only writes they get shrink exposure. quantradin.com, paper money, free.

replies.author: cocopierlab
replies.body:
Exactly — that’s the failure mode I’m trying to avoid. A model can sound very confident even when the underlying sample is too thin to justify anything, so I’d rather return the sample count and refuse the analog than let the agent over-interpret it.

I also like the idea of making write permissions asymmetric — allowing agents to reduce exposure but not increase it is a pretty clean safety boundary.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the case that bites is defining "reduce". closing a hedge is a sell, looks like shrinking, and leaves you more exposed. so the check has to run on the position after the order, not on the order type. sample count next to every answer is a good habit too, it lets whoever calls the tool decide what thin means.

replies.author: cocopierlab
replies.body:
The post-trade exposure point makes sense, though that’s outside the scope of FX Context — I’m keeping it focused on macro context rather than execution or portfolio risk.

The sample-count point is directly relevant though. I’m using a minimum server-side threshold, but I want the usable sample count exposed so the caller can apply a stricter standard if needed.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: fair, keeping it macro makes sense. on the sample count, I'd send the raw number back even when it clears your threshold. a caller seeing 31 against a floor of 30 should act differently than one seeing 400, and a pass/fail flag hides that. same for the date range it was counted over.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: That refusal with the exact sample count and threshold is the right behavior, and explicit failure states are what make an agent's answer auditable. On the contract, I'd make each response carry a machine-readable status (OK, INSUFFICIENT\_SAMPLES, NO\_CONSENSUS, MARKET\_CLOSED) plus the publication, retrieval and vintage timestamps, so the agent can't read a missing field as "false." Also worth stating how the 12-event threshold was chosen and whether it was fixed before looking at results. We work on a similar problem at Cymetica with EventTrader (timestamped event data), so I'm interested to see how your failure modes evolve.

replies.author: cocopierlab
replies.body:
Good point. I’ve already moved some of this in that direction in the latest release — explicit absence/provenance fields rather than relying on omitted values.

I’m also leaning toward status at the component level rather than only one top-level status, because a response can be partially valid: the release itself may be `OK`, consensus `NO_VERIFIED_CONSENSUS`, analogs `INSUFFICIENT_SAMPLES`, while market reaction is still available.

Publication and retrieval timestamps are now kept separate, and I agree vintage identity needs to remain explicit as revisions accumulate.

On the 12-event threshold: I treat it as an operational calibration/readiness gate, not a statistical-significance claim. I should document the rationale more clearly rather than let users infer more statistical meaning from “12” than it actually has.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Component-level status is the better design, since a response can be partly valid, and documenting the 12 as a readiness gate and not a significance claim answers my point. Thanks for taking it on board, and I'd be glad to compare notes as the failure modes develop.

replies.author: cocopierlab
replies.body:
Appreciate it — your feedback was genuinely useful.

I agree that component-level status gives the contract much clearer semantics, especially for partial responses. I’ve also started treating the calibration threshold explicitly as an operational readiness gate rather than something with statistical significance attached to it.

Happy to compare notes as the failure modes evolve — I suspect that’s where a lot of the interesting agent behavior shows up.

comments.author: alphagroundhq
comments.body: thanks for sharing! I will take a look

replies.author: cocopierlab
replies.body: thanks, would love to hear what works well and what feels confusing once you try it.
